title: When is the domination polynomial of a random graph ultra-log-concave?
description:
Unrefereed research candidate. A set of vertices of a graph is dominating when every vertex is in the set or adjacent to it. Counting dominating sets by size gives the coefficients of the domination polynomial. A sequence is log-concave if each term squared is at least the product of its neighbours; it then rises to a single peak and falls. Cameron (2019) checked all graphs with at most nine vertices, found exactly one whose domination polynomial is not log-concave (it fails because 7×7 < 1×50), and asked whether almost all graphs have a log-concave domination polynomial.

Results. (1) In the Erdős–Rényi graph G(n,p) with p ≤ 1−ε and p(log n)2 → ∞, with probability tending to one the proportion of k-sets that dominate is log-concave in k over the whole range (ultra-log-concavity), which implies log-concavity of the counts; the inequalities are strict exactly between the domination number and n minus the minimum degree. At p = 1/2 this shows that almost all graphs, labelled or unlabelled, have an ultra-log-concave and hence log-concave domination polynomial, answering Cameron's question. (2) The scale p(log n)2 → ∞ is the right one for a guarantee valid along every density sequence: for each finite limit θ there are explicitly tuned densities at which both properties fail with an explicit positive limiting probability, given by a Poisson law for the number of smallest dominating sets (at θ = 0 and λ = log 2 the limit is 1/2). (3) For the natural density p = θ/(log n)2 the probability of log-concavity has no limit: it tends to one along a set of n of density one but has liminf at most exp(−e−θ). (4) A binomial convex-order bound for the size of a weighted random dominating set follows.

Mechanism. The first nonzero count fluctuates like a Poisson variable, the next counts are huge and concentrated, and the curvature of the mean profile at the second nonzero coefficient is of order p(log n)2. In the upper range a deterministic second-difference inequality for overlapping neighbourhood complements takes over.

Limits. The results are asymptotic with no explicit n. Very dense graphs (p → 1) and sparser densities (p(log n)2 → 0) are not covered. Convergence at the boundary scale is slow. The finite computations (exhaustive for n ≤ 6, 20,000 seeded samples of G(n,1/2) for 7 ≤ n ≤ 18) are illustrations, not proofs.

Contents. The paper (LaTeX source and PDF) and five Python scripts with their recorded outputs: verify.py and audit_checks.py (exact checks of the mean formula, the hypergeometric identity and the tail inequality, and boundary thresholds), check_tuning.py (the tuned densities), finite_n.py (the table of failures for n ≤ 18) and natural_density.py (the slow-convergence illustration). Each script exits with an error on any failed check, also under python -O. Also included: the bibliography, a machine-readable index, a research-gate record, a review summary, a replay receipt and SHA-256 sums.

Assurance. Written proofs with finite computer checks. Internal AI-assisted review only: a combined five-role Claude review panel, one revision round with extensions, a verification re-review with a proof audit of every new or rewritten proof, and a clean replay with negative controls. No Astra/Codex review took place. This is not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Creator: Anonymous. Text CC0-1.0; code MIT.
